Who will be subject to the regulation or policy? • Defining the players who will be directly affected by regulation or policy is a key issue.

In principle, the answer to this question is easy - those whose behavior one wishes to change in order to deal with the risks or potential risks. • It is important to accurately define who is included in this definition - too broad an application will affect groups that are irrelevant, and a narrow application will impair the effectiveness of regulation or policy.
A good definition will reduce the possibility of various players deliberately removing themselves from the regulation.
Example: The basic definition in the Income Tax Ordinance is that only individuals (or companies) must pay taxes to the Israeli tax authorities if they are residents of Israel.
Tax planning is designed to enable taxpayers to evade tax obligations.

One such prominent method in tax planning is to establish a company in a tax haven (a foreign country where there is a preferred tax regime), while continuing business activity in the country of origin.
In this case, the taxpayer evades the application of Israel's tax laws.
In order to deal with this phenomenon, the Income Tax Ordinance includes the "Control and Management Test".
This determines whether the control and management of the business of a foreign company is executed from Israel.
If it is found so, the company is deemed a resident of Israel and accordingly is required to pay taxes in Israel.
At this stage, it is also important to set exceptions to the definition - groups which the regulation or policy need not apply to, or groups where the application is partial.
For example, it can be determined that burdensome regulatory directives need not apply to small businesses (see Annex I).

If the provisions are intended to apply to foreign corporations (for example: foreign investors) they must be written in English and in compliance with the regulations and policies of foreign countries.

Impact on work processes and business processes - Use process standards or performance standards?

There are two main ways to influence behavior: performance and design standards. (4) Performance standards determine the required result.
For example, the maximum level of bacteria in food or the maximum amount of time required to evacuate a building in an emergency; They do not define how the desired result will be achieved.
In contrast, design standards determine how to act - what technology to use, what are the work processes, how to build a structure and what actions are to be taken in a business.
Design standards do not deal with the outcome and can be met (by performing the necessary processes or using the required equipment) without reaching intended outcome of the regulation.
Performance standards define goals and objectives that must be met.
They are usually based on measuring performance in achieving a desired outcome.
The performance standard measures compliance regulatory objective (a safe product is manufactured, tap water is clean, etc.).
The manner of compliance with performance standards is flexible.
Performance standards require meeting targets and do not define a binding way to do so.
The strictness level of performance standards is based on a balance between the objective of risk mitigation and the practical and economic possibility of meeting the outcome.
The objective performance standard not to prevent damage, but an end characteristic and measurement of a process, product, or service.
Design standards require the use of a defined process, personnel, equipment or technology.
To address risk, design standards require the public to comply with specific directives and do not require it to meet the desired results.
The process approach of design standards is less flexible as it requires defined operations to be carried out in a specific manner.

It is possible to add flexibility to design standards if the decision maker defines a wide range of permissible methods and technologies, but most design standards include a single binding technical/process option.

Illustrative example: Fire safety A design standard determines the required equipment (fire extinguisher on each floor) and the engineering content of the building (location several emergency staircases, permitted and forbidden construction materials, window size, etc.).
The performance standard requires a design enabling all occupants to be evacuated within two minutes.
It will allow the engineer to design the building in a way that meets the performance standard (location of the emergency staircase, type of fire equipment, etc.) in a manner that can be proved.
The main limitation of performance standards is that they require a measurable goal and compliance with the goal can be determined.
For example, when wishing to determine a performance standard for being free of disease x, there must be a reliable and available test for pathogens of disease x.
The selection of design standards has three drawbacks that must be considered: • First, the use of design standards creates high degree government involvement in the content of business processes.
This entails extensive involvement and the imposition of costs on supervised entities.

As result, changing or updating the requirements imposes significant costs on the public due to factors such as replacing equipment or changing the work method (it is easier to adapt to changes in performance standards).

Design standards require many resources from the government regulator: addressing numerous details, updating requirements and, of course, extensive supervision of each of the requirements. • Second, design standards suppress innovation and prevent preparation for new problems.
As the public and businesses are committed to the process defined, design standards do not enable them to adopt new solutions and technologies cope any unforeseen risks.
Therefore, design standards prevent operational streamlining and improvement of safety levels.
Performance standards enable the supervised sector to find a solution encourages competition and innovation.

In the world of performance standards, if in the future a new risk arises, or new technology becomes available - the supervised entities will readjust accordingly in order to comply with the performance standard.

The design process does enable this. • Third, design standards may give preference to the technology or work method of a particular factor, thereby affixing the economy and providing a regulatory advantage to certain players.
Performance standards and design standards can be used both in a permits and licenses regime and in a norms regime.

Example: Licensing the driving of a motor vehicle License with design standards: In order to obtain a driver's license, attending a minimum 28 practical lessons with a driving instructor is mandatory; License with performance standards: In order to obtain a driver's license, it is necessary to prove the control of the vehicle (practical exam).

Example: Binding norms for sanitation in public pools Binding norm with design standards: In a public swimming pool, use of water filtering and disinfecting system is mandatory; Binding norm with performance standards: In a public pool no more than 10 general coliform bacteria in 100 ml of water is permitted.
It is important to clarify the distinction between design standards performance standards not to confuse them.
For example, a regulator responsible for food safety is debating whether to demand the cleaning of a factory floor twice a day or to demand that the factory floor be clean and dry.
Although the second requirement is formulated as a result, both options are a design standard aimed at reducing the risk of food contamination.
The performance standard relates to compliance with the regulatory objectives: food safety and health (for example, the number of harmful bacteria in the finished product).
When policy or regulation defines the means to achieve the regulatory objectives then it is a design standard rather than a performance standard.

To whom or to what will the regulation or public policy refer? • Regulation (prohibitions, obligations and conditions) and public policy (instructions, benefits, requirements, etc.) can refer to elements of three main types: people, actions, and objects.
People - for example, to require an individual (who meets a certain definition) to take action or to refrain from taking it, to have certain skills, etc.
Benefits can also be granted on this basis (for example, tax benefits for women).
This group also includes groups and corporations.
Actions (or processes) - example, to determine prohibited actions, actions that must be carried out, or defining how certain actions should be carried out.

Objects (including equipment and technology) - for example, determine equipment must be maintained, the level of maintenance equipment, or prohibiting the use of defined objects. • For each element of the regulatory content, it should be defined whether it applies to people, actions, or objects.
The choice should be based on the risk assessment that has been carried out.
An identification must be made as to whether risk mitigation will be achieved by focusing on people, action, or objects.
Illustrative example: In order to address the risk of accidents on construction sites, it is necessary to identify the cause of the risk or its severity.
If the accidents occur because of the recklessness of intoxicated workers - the focus should be on the human factor.
If accidents occur due carelessness when operating the crane - the focus should be on the regulation of activities.
If the accidents occur due to improper equipment or improperly maintained equipment - focus should be placed on the state of the equipment.
It is possible to formulate almost identical rules, difference between them being the element to which they relate.

Untargeted treatment will not be effective.
Supervision and enforcement will deal with objects that have been defined in the content of the regulation or policy.

Illustrative example: One must ensure that equipment is maintained at a satisfactory level.
A rule focused on action can be determined: for example, maintenance must be performed once every six months.
It is it is possible to determine a rule focused on equipment: the equipment must be maintained in proper working order.
Both rules are similar and have the same purpose, but they have different content.
They impose different compliance costs on the public and the scope of the supervision and enforcement activities will be affected by this choice.
Focusing on treatment of risk and limiting intervention • It is important that the regulatory or policy content be focused on the problem and not exceed the minimum required to address the risk.
Any government involvement may impose costs - including unexpected costs and effects.
The best way to minimize undesirable effects is to focus the content only on the treatment of risks.
It is important to define exactly what the problem is (the mechanism of risk creation, reasons for the severity problem) to ensure the government tool focuses only on them.
It is easy to set sweeping rules, but they also impose restrictions on activities that do not contribute to risk.
Example: When driving in the dark, it is necessary to use the lighting installed in the vehicle.
Many countries (including Israel) have identified that some power 100 101

Therefore, the regulation states that every vehicle must have two headlights - one that illuminates using a high light and the other using a low light (Section 334 of the Israeli Traffic Regulations, 5721 - 1961).
Over the years, advanced lighting systems have been developed, allowing for high-light illumination all the time.
An automatic control system identifies other vehicles selectively weakens the intensity of the light at the angle of the other vehicle (for example, https://goo.gl/QQDyFk).
Current regulation prevents adoption of the new technology.
If the regulation had focused on the problem (ensuring lighting and preventing glare), the adoption of new solutions would have been possible.
Instead the decision was to use a detailed definition (there must be two separate headlights with different characteristics) which prevents the implementation of another solution.

Guiding questions for developing a regime of permits and licenses Which factors require a license, and which actions require a permit?

In contrast, a permit is permission to carry out an action, and accordingly is generally limited to one use.
It is therefore necessary to examine whether the goal is to supervise every action in advance, or the factors that carry out the actions.
Choosing to use licenses over permits significantly reduces the burden on the public. • It is necessary to examine how often a license should be renewed (how long is it valid for?).
The answer to this depends on the frequency at which there are systemic factual or legal changes that require the license expires, and the licensee contact the issuer.

Illustrative example: A well-known anecdote tells of the period of colonial rule in India.
The British sought to reduce the number of cobra snakes on the streets of Delhi.
It was decided to give a reward for each dead cobra snake collected.

At first it seemed that the new policy was achieving its goal, but later on the British discovered that many Indians recognized there was a "demand" for dead cobras and therefore began to grow and breed cobras in order to collect the reward.
When the British became aware of this, they revoked the reward policy.
As a result, the snake growers released the cobras from their breeding farms, and the city of Delhi was flooded with cobras.

The first mistake the British made, at the policy-making stage, was the failure to recognize that monetary compensation cobras would not necessarily stimulate hunting of snakes but would result in their institutionalized growth.
The second mistake was the lack of understanding of the decision to revoke the reward policy on the behavior of snake breeders.

After completing the process and choosing the desired solution and content, a trial run of the regulation or policy should be implemented on a limited scale and for a fixed period - for example, by publishing a "temporary order".

The pilot allows for the empirical testing of the risk management, and for determining whether it is effective in dealing with the risk (and what are the government costs and costs to the public as a result).
It is important to define in advance criteria and outcome indices for evaluating the trial run, and to establish a mechanism for collecting and analyzing data during the trial run period.
A pilot run is especially important when it comes to regulation or policy with extensive social or economic impact.
Limiting validity and periodic examination.
Even after the pilot run, it is recommended to limit in advance the validity of the selected regulation or policy.

One can assume with certainty that in the future, circumstances will change - risks will arise, new risks will disappear or change, a new method (regulatory, business or technological) will be developed for dealing with the risks, etc.
Unlike the budget, which is often examined, policies and regulations anchored in laws, regulations and procedures, are not examined once every specified period and are not required to be re-ratified.
It is recommended to limit the validity of the decision.
This will assist the system in the future, ensuring the system updates the risk management and will not rely on a process carried out in the distant past.
The customary way to do this is through "sunset clauses" which presuppose that the law, regulation or procedure will be valid, for a defined period.
Towards the end of the period, a renewed risk management process will be conducted, and based on the updated risk assessment, updated decisions will be made.

This step strengthens the decision maker as it maintains the flexibility of the government system in the future (in view of the inherent difficulty in changing laws and regulations that have no effect). 112 113
To date, the process has dealt with early steps aimed at pro-actively reducing the probability of the risk occurring or mitigating its severity.
In contrast, Crisis Management/Contingency Planning deals with risk management once it has been realized.
Preparing respond risks retrospectively is especially important when dealing with high severity risks.

A successful crisis management system will prepare the system for risks mapped at the risk identification stage, but also for dealing with new risks and risks that have not been identified. main challenge crisis management is that the system is required to act quickly, under conditions of stress and uncertainty.
These are challenging conditions for making decisions.
The target in crisis management is to reach as high a level of readiness as possible prior to any risk occurring.
This enables decision-makers to determine what form of action is best and that all necessary resources will be ready.

When there are clear guidelines for all functionaries and all equipment and resources are prepared, if the crisis occurs, everything will be ready for implementation, thus reducing the risk of errors in the exercise of discretion.
Crisis management is a continuation of the process of assessment and early treatment of risks.
It also complements them.
Crisis management can be a major strategy for dealing with risks.
The decision maker may choose a risk acceptance strategy (not to act in advance to mitigate the risk) and prepare to treat it retroactively.
In addition, crisis management can be part of a risk mitigation strategy based on insurance methods.

Crisis management enables the system to recover from the risk damage, but it requires dedicating resources advance (planning, training, purchasing equipment) - similar to the purchase of an insurance policy.
Therefore, crisis management especially necessary for risks of a high level of severity and can be a major tool when severity is high, and probability low.
Crisis management entails early preparation (preparation "contingency plans" and resources in times of need) and real-time response actions.
Since this process is designed to provide a response to risks - it should be performed soon after the Risk Assessment.

Crisis management is designed to deal with damage and to ensure functional continuity in disaster situations - both of the government unit and other vital functions (such as public infrastructure or business).
A key component of crisis management is prior coordination with other entities and joint preliminary preparations.
If the event materializes, the various bodies will be required to act in unison, while being familiar with the division of powers and functions between them.

In Israel, the main emergency bodies include National Emergency Authority, the Home Front Command, the Emergency Economy Department, the hospitals, the National Fire and Rescue Authority and Magen David Adom (Israel's official ambulance service, blood service and disaster rescue agency).
The key stages of treating the risk that has occurred, should be the key points of the crisis management contingency plan.
As with any significant decision, it is preferable to examine the steps that will be taken after comparing alternatives and conducting a cost- benefit analysis.

In addition to the three risk treatment stages, it is important to prepare CRISIS MANAGEMENT the regulation and public policy so there are appropriate powers and methods of action for operation during the crisis.

Preparation may include the option of making policy or regulation more stringent (taking extra caution in implementing the rules or operating the supervision and enforcement system in times of crisis) and facilitating policy or regulation (removing barriers to improve crisis management and recovery).
Illustrative example: Authority to ease regulatory or policy requirements During an outbreak, vaccines and medicines are needed.

In preparing for such an event, it was decided to determine in advance that the director of the unit has the authority to allow accelerated licensing of drugs and vaccines without undergoing all the usual tests and procedures.
This temporary measure will be activated in times of crisis, in order to enable crisis management and recovery.

Illustrative example: Authority to make regulatory or policy requirements more stringent At times of a suspected unusual security or safety incident involving civil aviation, it is necessary to isolate the dangerous aircrafts and evacuate all aircrafts from Israeli airspace.
Therefore, it must be determined in advance that the director of the Airports Authority has the power to order all civilian aircrafts to land immediately.
This provision expands the powers of the government to limit activities that involve or are associated with risk.
It is not intended for routine use, but only in exceptional emergency situations.
Immediate response: stabilization of the situation and urgent treatment Lifesaving operations - search and rescue, evacuation medical treatment.
It is necessary to define what actions should be carried out, how, who is responsible for executing them, and to allocate resources in advance for these actions.
Example: "Magen David Adom" is the State of Israel's national rescue organization for emergency medicine.
The existence and activity of the organization is intended to save lives after a risk has been realized.
Delineating the source of the damage and preventing the expansion of the damage's effect.
The planning must include how to treat the cause of damage in order to contain its reach.
For example, in the case of an epidemic, it is necessary to locate patients and carriers who may infect their environment.
In addition, a plan must be prepared to contain the effects of the damage on the protected assets.
In the example of an epidemic this would include vaccination of the population within a defined radius around the risk epicenter.
Communicating the event.
Guidelines on how to act and provide information about the risk should be prepared in advance.
Communication channels and the way the messages are conveyed (written, visual, through senior official interview) must be considered.
It is important the guidelines and explanations to the public be adapted to emergencies in a clear, simple and immediate way. 114 115
Example: In 2016, National Emergency Authority began preparations possible occurrence of a tsunami event.
The preparations included the preparation of escape routes from the beaches and the deployment of warning and guidance signs.
These actions are intended to enable a better response to the risk that has been realized.

Actions required to prevent further injury.
Preparation for any further action required to prevent additional damage.

Contingency plans should include instructions for specific actions for each critical unit in the system.
These instructions are intended to prevent the disruption of essential services and infrastructures.
Example: Israel Electric Corporation is preparing to operate power plants following rare events such as accidents and natural disasters.

Special facilities should prepared use emergencies, as well as work methods equipment emergency situations.
An example of this is the provision of flashlights in the event of a power failure.

These facilities and methods will be used as an alternative to facilities and methods used in the routine - for example, in the event of a crisis, accelerated procurement processes can be performed without a tender committee.
They are also necessary serve emergency activities for the treatment of risk (for example, installing generators to supply electricity to a war room established in the field).
Pre-planning of the deployment and operation of alternative infrastructure (for example, communications infrastructure) may be required at times.

Risk may disrupt the provision of essential services to the public or a defined group.
Preparations must be made in advance for the supply of electricity, water, fuel, food, medical services, medical equipment and other essential services.
At times it is necessary for emergency supplies to be prepared and maintained.
Conclusion of the event: Rehabilitation and return to routine At this stage, actions will be taken to restore activity to routine.
This process may take several weeks.
Since this process also requires dedication of resources and attention, it is advisable to prepare for it in advance.
The conclusion of the event is defined as a situation in which the relevant activity returns to normal function, as it was prior to the occurrence of the risk.
At the conclusion of the event it is important to conduct a professional enquiry of the event, led by the managerial level.
The enquiry is integrated into the organization's control system (detailed in following chapters).
The main role of the enquiry is to identify and treat faulty processes in order to prevent the realization of future risks.
It is important to conduct an enquiry regarding rules and work processes, rather than focus on the responsibility of one factor or another. 116 117
Risk communication includes transfer of information from the government decision maker to the relevant stakeholders and the public.
The explanations in this chapter are suggestions and not a substitute for effective and productive working systems already in place with the government spokesperson's office.
The instructions of the spokespersons must be on a case-by-case basis.
The decision maker's goal is to manage the risk optimally according to the principle maximum aggregate welfare.
This is done by influencing public behavior.
To ensure maximum effectiveness, it important provide the public (or relevant groups within it) with information about the risks and the government policy for addressing them.
Risk communication is carried out throughout the risk management process: from the Risk Assessment stage, through the Risk Treatment stage and during the implementation of the selected policy.

Risk communication has three main objectives: • To create public awareness of risks; • To instruct the public on how to act in order to avoid or mitigate risk; • To present and explain government policy - what risks it addresses (and how) and what risks it does not address.
Since communication public can influence its conduct, risk communication can serve as an advanced regulation method for risk management.
For example, if the public believes a significant risk is a negligible risk, it is possible transfer and explanations will change the public's perception conduct on the subject.
For both individuals and organizations, information is a fundamental element in the decision- making processes.
Proper use of this tool can have a material effect on the public's exposure to risks.
Example: The public mistakenly thinks that an airplane is a dangerous vehicle and that private vehicles are a safer mode of transportation.
In practice, the situation is reversed - an airplane is a much safer vehicle.
The public misunderstands the probability of occurrence of the various risks.
The consequence is the public fears the use of airplanes, resulting in excessive use of cars - a behavior that increases the risk to the traveling public.
Illustrative example: Parents think children get lice from playing in a sandbox.
In actuality, lice are mainly transferred through contact with dogs and cats.
In this case, the parenting community misunderstands circumstances in which there is high exposure to risk.
As a result, they may be ill-prepared to prevent and treat the risk.
It recommended check retrospectively whether communication has achieved its purpose.
The accepted process for this is through surveys / questionnaires, in which the public is asked how it CRISIS MANAGEMENT understands the risks and the risk management policy.

The goal is to equip the public with relevant information that the decision maker has collected and analyzed.
Communicating the risk assessment has two main principles: communicating the message clearly and providing clear guidelines for action.
In order to help the public to act correctly in face of the risk, it is important the communication of the risk assessment includes practical instruction on how the public should act.

In the first stage, it is necessary to clarify the public's position: • How familiar is the public with the risk? • What experience does the public have in exposure to the risk? • How does the public assess the severity of the damage from the risk and the probability of its realization? • What other characteristics does the public attribute to the risk?

The target audience must be accurately defined. • In what way must the information be disseminated in order for it to be received and understood by the public and its target audience? (I.e., length of the message; how information is transmitted: visual message, warning, training, publication of press release). • When should the information be distributed and how often should an update be released? • How should the public act?
What actions to avoid, what actions are vital, etc.

• There is value in giving the public information about the decision to treat or not treat certain risks.

The first set of such events includes a change in risk - the disappearance of a risk, the appearance of new risks, or a change in the risk profile (change in probability, severity, or circumstances that characterize the risk).
A second set of events for which information should be provided includes activities, enforcement violation of government policy.
Communicating these events is important in order to explain what the government is doing to implement its policy.

An example of which may be informing the public that the supervisory system is active and that violators are apprehended and punished in a manner that promotes deterrence. • Another case of communicating risks during policy execution is if the risk materializes.
The guiding principle in these situations is to provide the public with clear and concise information that can be easily processed and used in an emergency situation if the occurs.

Complex, lengthy messages or messages phrased in professional language, will not be understood, and of no or little benefit to the public. • When the risk is realized, the manner in which the government responds is significant.
There are a variety of possible responses to a risk that has been realized.

These include refraining from providing information until the completion enquiry, through gradual provision of information culminating an immediate notification acknowledging responsibility for the occurrence.

As part of the broad concept of risk management, it is proposed to formulate the message to the public according to the following principles: It important provide information to the public, as long as the information is reliable, and its publication will not damage crisis management operations.

Since there no zero-risk situations, it important clarify that the risk occurrence is not necessarily the result of a government failure to completely prevent risks, but that the risk exists as part of the activity of the parties involved.
Even during an event, it must be remembered and noted that the occurrence of a risk does not mean the policy or regulation has failed.
At the time of the risk's actualization and shortly thereafter, there is a tendency to look for those responsible for the event.
It is important to conduct the review in a responsible manner and not publish unfounded assumptions.
This principle applies both when the blame is directed at the government and when it is directed at private entities.
A debrief is an internal professional tool and is also a control mechanism against publication unfounded information.

Risk management and enforcement is the continuation of risk management in developing regulation and public policy.
The process developing regulation and public policy defines the general framework, which consists of binding requirements and sanctions in respect of their violation.
This chapter deals with the supervision and enforcement system.

This system determines how to use the policy-defined tools to ensure compliance with the requirements - for example, decisions regarding what actions are to be taken, vis-à-vis whom, and with what frequency.

Once the risks have been identified and the methods for treating them have been determined, it is necessary to decide how to ensure compliance with the regulation or the policy established, in order to mitigate risks.
The meta-goal of the supervision and enforcement system is to encourage and ascertain regulatory or policy compliance.
Noncompliance may arise from the supervised entities' lack of incentive or inability to comply with the requirements or ignorance of their existence.

Therefore, the supervision system includes traditional actions such as data collection, inspections enforcement (imposition sanctions), alongside actions guiding the supervised entities on how to meet the prescribed requirements.
The role of the regulator and the responsibility supervised entities.

According OECD guidance, it should be made clear - in law, in procedures and in practice - that the primary responsibility for complying with regulation and not taking inordinate risks lies with the supervised entities.

The role of regulators and inspectors is to assist and promote compliance, but they are not responsible for regulatory compliance by the supervised entities or for preventing risks, as they are not the supervised entities.
The regulator's job is to set rules, guide the supervised entities and penalize in cases of noncompliance.
The supervised entities should be given responsibility for compliance with the requirements and for the risks they pose to the public.

If risk management is performed at the regulation or policy-setting stage, the risks tackled will already be defined and characterized and the supervision and enforcement system GENERAL development process will be simpler.

If risk management is not performed at the regulation or policy-setting stage, developing the supervision and enforcement system will necessitate the collection of data and evaluation of the different risks and violations.
Risk management in supervision and enforcement is essentially similar to risk management in the development of regulation and public policy.

Both are based on an attribute analysis of the problem (noncompliance or public risk), adaptation of government handling measures to the problem's attributes, prioritization problems by degree of importance.
Planning enforcement system is based on the criteria of probability and severity: the probability of a violation being committed and the contribution of the requirement to damage mitigation.

Nevertheless, management in supervision and enforcement is simpler, as it is should be a routine work process used by supervision and enforcement units on a daily basis (supervision and enforcement are routinely performed actions, as distinct from policy-setting).
This following model presents a guide for the planning and operation of a supervision and enforcement system.
The model is based on the mapping of the attributes of the supervised entities and requirements and on the rating of each pairing of a requirement with the supervised entities.
The model is suitable a considerable portion of the supervision and enforcement tasks.
However, some situations may require a different model.
For example, there may be cases where the more appropriate approach would be to rate each supervised entity (business, buildings, shipments, etc.) by a dedicated set of criteria.
The model in this Guide is a baseline.
It is advisable to use a computerized system management supervision and enforcement actions.
Computerized systems have predictive capability, based on machine learning, statistical analysis and professional information.
Automation digitization of the supervision system will help to weight a multitude of data, ensure consistency, uniformity and facilitate the inspectors' work.

Negligible risk.

After the initial screening, a list should be made of all the requirements.
Each requirement should be assessed for how much it decreases the probability and severity of the risk.
A "requirement" can be an isolated or a set of requirements directed at a single supervised entity for dealing with a single risk.
Some requirements affect both the probability and severity, while others affect only one of the two variables.

Probability: To what extent does full compliance with a requirement influence the probability of risk occurrence?
Severity: To what extent will damage severity be reduced by full compliance with a requirement?

The key advantage of complaint-based supervision is that the supervision and enforcement system focuses resources on handling violations that have occurred and not on searching for violations that may or may not occur.
A traditional supervision system assumes some of the supervised entities will be found violating the requirements, while some will be found complying with the requirements.
A complaint-based supervision system directs part of the resources to tasks with a high probability of finding only supervised entities that are violating the requirements.
A further advantage of complaint- based supervision is its focus on violations that create public risk or damage.
Traditional supervision is likely to focus on technical or negligible violations that do not significantly influence the public risk exposure.
Complaint-based directed at handling violations that create public risk, damage or disturbance, since otherwise no complaint would have been filed.
Complaint-based supervision screens out violations that have no complaint filed against them - technical violations or violations of formal requirements that do not bother the public.

Employing complaint-based supervision is particularly appropriate and effective when it concerns a public that is aware of the requirements and can actively report violations, and when public violations are credible (a minimal number of false complaints and consistent and uniform reporting).

First, complaint-based likely to be biased due to reliance on external complaints.
The bias could arise from false complaints and from a lack of uniformity in the method of filing the complaints (non-reporting populations, cases that go unreported, etc.).

Second, there are violations that necessitate proactive supervision in order to discover and expose them (for example, at the criminal level: offenses of possession receipt stolen property, offenses of extortion and blackmail, offenses of drug use, etc.).
Such offenses are generally not discovered through complaints received from the public.
Third, under this mechanism, supervision is exercised only after the violation has been discovered.

Therefore, it is suitable only in cases where the violation is retroactively identifiable (an ongoing violation or a violation with a retroactively identifiable result), and unsuitable for violations that must be identified real-time.
Fourth, complaint- based supervision is appropriate for handling violations of binding norms, but inappropriate for supervision and enforcement of permits and licenses.

While the supervision system is in operation, it is advisable to explore the use of alternative tools as necessary, and not be limited to the use of a single tool, namely: exercising control over compliance with requirements; conducting instruction sessions for supervised entities (how and why to comply with requirements); and communicating the risk and its treatment measures to the supervised entities and the public.

In the event noncompliance is the result of deliberate criminality, traditional supervisory action must be executed to ensure that enforcement and punishment provide a deterrent for the supervised entity.

Consolidation Supervision Activities In establishing the supervision system, it is important to take into account the bureaucratic actions deriving from the creation of the system (issuance of approvals/ notices of violation, taking laboratory samples, etc.).
Likewise, it should be established whether there are supervision actions that can be joined with other government actions that are being carried out in connection with the same supervised entities.
This may spare the need for especially carrying out supervision.
Moreover, there should be a focus on supervision actions that address a broader set of requirements.
There are supervision actions that enable monitoring several requirements.
For example: when arriving at the production plant to conduct an inspection, it is possible to examine both the products themselves and the plant workers' familiarity with the requirements.
On the other hand, if in an inspection is conducted at the product shipping stage, there may be no plant workers present and thus their knowledge cannot be evaluated.
Generally, every government entity has its own separate supervision system (the "silo" effect, meaning a narrow, inward-looking attitude).

Therefore, every supervised entity is subject to a number of separate supervision and enforcement systems (for example - a plant is subject to the supervision of the Health Ministry, Labor Ministry, Environmental Protection Ministry, etc.).
As a result, the government system devotes overlapping resources execution activities.

Such situations involve a waste of resources for all entities: double costs for the supervised entity (devoting time several inspections), double supervision actions, and splitting of information on the supervised entity among several entities.
Consolidation or combination of supervision and enforcement actions leads to a savings of much needed resources and raises the effectiveness of the supervision system.
Hence, the aim should be to unify clusters of supervision actions and execute them as a consolidated whole.
Consolidated activity includes the conduct of inspections, checks, examinations and instruction sessions in respect of a range of requirements and areas.

This can be done by setting up mechanisms for coordination and collaboration among units operating in allied areas and vis-à- vis similar supervised entity groups (e.g., supervision of the engineering design of power plants is carried out by both the Energy Ministry and the Labor Ministry).
Such collaborations augment the capabilities of both supervision systems and enhance their capacity for control, instruction and enforcement vis-à-vis the supervised entities.
Illustrative example: Environmental regulation of chemical plants includes provisions regarding wastewater, emission of air pollutants, water purification treatment hazardous materials.
Each of the four topics include different requirements relating to a different activity in the plant.

Supervision of each topic within a separate inspection framework, by a separate supervision unit, results in a waste of resources of the supervision system (four different inspectors arriving at the plant to conduct an inspection).

Moreover, each inspector will be exposed only to the hits associated with the specific topic they are supervising and will not see the complete picture and the mutual effects of compliance or noncompliance with the various requirements.
Integrated inspection enables streamlining the system, strengthens the supervising entity and achieves greater effectiveness.
An advanced way to consolidate supervision activities is to establish an integrated inspection system with structural unification.
The framework of this includes a unit set up for performing integrated inspection on behalf of several authorities and government ministries.
Example: In 2017, Malta enacted Coordination Government Inspections Act.
Pursuant to the law, the Inspections Coordination Office was set up.
According to the law, the purpose of the move was two-fold - the reduction of costs imposed on the supervised entities and the promotion of transparency and effectiveness of the supervision actions.

The law, inter alia, empowers the Inspections Coordination Office to instruct the authorities how consolidate their supervision resources, issue binding standards regarding the manner of carrying out the supervision actions set up common database for the different supervisory authorities.

The law applies to 23 regulatory entities in various fields, such as: Commission for the Rights of Persons with Disability, Regulator for Energy and Water Services, Tourism Authority, Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority, and Plant Health Directorate.

Uniformity Consistency Operating the Supervision System A common problem among supervision systems is the lack of uniformity and consistency in the inspectors' work.
For example, when two inspectors interpret the requirements differently, they end up presenting different requirements to the supervised entities.
This impairs the ability to achieve the regulation or policy objectives (since some of the inspectors are deviating from the policy).
This gives rise to variability among different supervised entities.
Furthermore, same supervised entity is likely to run into different requirements, according to the demands of the inspector who examined it.
A lack of uniformity and consistency lowers the compliance level of the supervised entities.
From their perspective the requirements are inconsistent, giving them no incentive to comply with them.
Non-uniformity and inconsistency make it difficult for the supervised entities to comply with the provisions, leaving the inspectors with the task of enforcing them effectively.

Typical causes for the lack of uniformity inconsistency are: multiple provisions (a long and detailed list of requirements); vagueness regarding the substance of the requirements; absence of written documents with a description of the requirements.
One of the most effective tools for contending with these problems is the issuance of a checklist by the supervision system.
The checklist must include all the requirements demanded of the supervised entities clearly emphasize core requirements - the principal and most important requirements risk mitigation.
The inspections will be carried out according to the checklist, and the latter will serve as the implementation document of the regulation or policy.
The checklist must be a closed list.
It should not be possible to introduce further requirements beyond original document.
Creating the checklist also helps the supervision system to know whether the requirement list is too long and detailed (which makes it difficult for the supervised entities to comply).
If it is, it may be decided to cut down requirements or simplify them, in order encourage compliance.

Use of a checklist helps manage system (ensures consistency and uniformity among the inspectors, enables measurement) and also lets the supervised entities know which provisions are the most important for risk-mitigation.

Example: The authorities in Lithuania make extensive use of checklists for purposes of supervision and enforcement. checklist sets out clearly all the provisions and requirements the supervised entities must meet, with the supervision actions carried out only in respect of the checklist's content.
Lithuania's experience demonstrates use of checklists solves one of the chief problems of the supervision systems: inconsistent non-uniform inspection.
Moreover, the checklist is useful when the inspectors are unable analyze risks themselves.
Checklist-based inspection limits the discretion of the inspectors and favors consistency over flexibility.
Use of the checklist helps clarify the requirements, encourages supervised entities to comply with the provisions and improves the supervision system.

It is useful to issue a checklist for each type of supervision action: inspection when receiving a business license, annual inspection, inspection of large businesses, inspection of high-risk businesses, etc.
It is important to update the checklist on a regular basis with the aid of the field workers.
The checklist should be issued along with guidelines, principles and tools for complying with requirements, as a complete whole aimed at promoting compliance with requirements.
These materials can serve as a basis for an instruction system that helps the entities supervise themselves and verify compliance with requirements.

Certainty and Clarity for Supervised Entities In addition uniformity consistency in the operation of the supervision system, it is important to ensure that the supervised parties understand what they are required to do.

This involves a fourfold problem, namely: multiplicity of requirements; dispersion requirements over numerous documents (regulations, procedures, guidelines and directives); requirements which are not set down in writing; and use of complex legal or professional language.
These factors make it difficult for all supervised parties to understand the requirements and comply with them.
This is especially so for new, one-time or small players.
The guiding principle is that the rules and processes of the supervision and enforcement system must be clear and public.
The duties of the supervised entity and the duties and responsibilities of the government units must be made public.
In particular, it is important to explain how the supervised entity will be examined and investigated.
There is no need to "reveal all the cards" and examination methods, but the supervised entity must know exactly what is expected of it and how it should prove compliance with the requirements.
The supervision system must be as transparent as possible.
The system will more effectively encourage compliance and deter violations if the supervised entities are aware of the mechanism that underlies the supervision and enforcement actions.
For example, if the supervision and enforcement system is based on the compliance record of the supervised entities, this is important knowledge that will promote compliance.
On the other hand, the detailed supervision EXECUTION OF SUPERVISION AND ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS 148 149 Supervision and Enforcement Supervision and Enforcement

Where the requirements or processes are complex, it is recommended to prepare a guide or manual for the supervised entities explains how to meet the requirements, what steps are advisable to take, how the requirements interrelate, what solutions exist for the treatment of risks, etc.
To ensure its usefulness, such a guide must be prepared as a joint project between the supervision system (headquarters field personnel) supervised entities.

Example: In the United Kingdom, the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) operates a project called "Health and Safety Made Simple," which issues clear and simple guidelines on health and safety at the workplace.
The project, among other things, explains the regulatory requirements and how the supervised business can identify risks to workers.
It also distributes posters and informational material to businesses.
Example: The British program "Safer Food, Better Business" (SFBB) is designed to help small and medium- sized businesses comply with the complex regulatory requirements in the food industry.
The program strives to improve the safety level in the industry and help supervised entities know whether they are operating in accordance with the requirements.

In the framework of the program, guides were issued various businesses food industry: restaurants, catering businesses, etc. guides contain step-by-step explanations, clear illustrations and examples of correct and incorrect ways of performing actions.
The guides were translated into the most widely spoken languages among workers in the United Kingdom's guest accommodation and catering sectors.
The guides can also set out approved implementation methods were examined in the past by the supervision system and found useful.
The publication of approved methods makes it clear to the supervised entities that anyone implementing the approved method is operating in accordance with the requirements.
This makes compliance easier for the supervised entities and encourages the use of effective risk treatment measures.

As part of the mechanism approved implementation methods, one can also remunerate supervised entities that take steps to improve compliance and mitigate risks - for example, reducing the number of supervision actions when the supervised entity implements risk treatment measures or operates an internal enforcement program in order to ensure compliance with the requirements.
Enhanced certainty clarity regarding supervision processes: To increase the level of certainty of the supervised entities, it is customary to issue a Service Level Agreement (SLA).

This document details; how the supervision unit "contracts" with the supervised entities, how information is provided in an efficient manner (answers to questions, instructions, solutions to problems, etc.), within how much time a supervised entity's communication is handled, what are the supervision processes, how the fine-imposition mechanisms operates and how to appeal a decision.
Since uncertainty lack clarity harm the supervised entities' compliance capacity, efficient handling of the questions posed by them contributes greatly to the compliance level.
A rapid response to questions and problems of supervised entities helps both to comply with the requirements and to understand the supervision system.
It also builds trust in the system.
It is advisable to document the questions and the answers provided.
When an important or recurring question is encountered, it should be written up and published with an official response.
Additionally, maintaining a follow-up of questions of the supervised entities is an excellent tool for identifying gaps in their understanding of the system.
If a certain issue raises numerous questions or disagreements, it obviously requires clarification.
Example: Israel Securities Authority (ISA) publishes its website answers to general questions posed by supervised entities, as well as responses to preliminary inquiries made on concrete issues.
The competent answers clarify the ISA's position on various issues.

The responses to the preliminary inquiries are published without identifying the party that submitted the inquiry, but they are detailed enough to elucidate to the supervised parties how the ISA enforces the law and the requirements.

It is highly recommended to set up a telephone support center, or appoint a public service officer in the regulatory unit, to serve as an authority who can be approached by business owners for information on compliance with regulatory requirements.
Supervision actions (such as inspections) reveal various gaps between the requirements and actual compliance by the supervised entities.
Therefore, at the conclusion of a supervision action it is important to advise the supervised entity (orally and in writing) on the matters requiring improvement.
It is also desirable to give instructions on how this should be done.
It is advisable to identify and focus on critical issues, given the limited resources of the supervision system and the supervised entities.

Additionally, it is recommended to adopt a certainty and stability code, according to which changes in the requirements and their interpretation will be made biannually at set times - for example, in the middle and end of the year.

This allows supervised entities a period of at least half a year without regulatory changes, thereby increasing clarity and certainty and improving their capacity to adapt their activity to the requirements.

Under this code, any change in the requirements will become effective only after each supervised entity has been given prior notice and allowed a period of at least three and a half months in which to organize and adapt to the new requirements.
Deterrent Proportionate Enforcement In the preface to the Guide, guidelines were set forth supervision, enforcement and deterrence.
The following explains how to operate enforcement system in order to achieve maximum deterrence.
Communication and explanation of the enforcement system.
When operating the enforcement system (imposition of administrative fines, filing of criminal indictments), it is important to explain the risk and the nature of the violation.

It is recommended to relate to the following four parameters: (1) the nature of the risk (severity, annual number of cases, annual damage to the national economy); (2) the nature of the violation and its influence on the realization of the risk; (3) the benefit accruing to the violating entity from the violation; (4) the degree of 150 151 Supervision and Enforcement Supervision and Enforcement
probability that violating entities will be caught.
It is especially important to explain this to the court, in order to be able to request the imposition of a sanction that will make the violation unprofitable for supervised entities.

Enforcement punishment adjusted for risk and compliance The sanction for a violation must be suited to the character of the violating entity, to the nature of the requirement and to the circumstances of the violation (extent of the risk's effect, number of violations, gain from committing the violation, and number of actions performed by the supervised entity).
The punitive system must take into account the balance between ensuring effective deterrence and encouraging future compliance.
A harsher punishment should be meted out for recurring violations by the same supervised entity (even if they are relatively minor violations).
Punishment should also be more stringent in the case of an isolated violation far-reaching implications.

The fact that the multiple violations are minor in nature, or the fact that the violation is a one-time occurrence, will be taken into account when determining the scope of the supervision, but not when deciding on the severity of the punishment.

There are supervised entities that may respond better to an administrative sanction (restriction activity, suspension of an activity permit) combined counseling appropriate conduct, whereas other supervised entities may be deterred only by the imposition of a criminal penalty.
One should take into account the size and financial robustness of each violating entity.
It should ensure effective deterrence, but not cause the collapse of small supervised entities.
It is also recommended to apply the principle, which has already been adopted in several countries, according to which sanctions should not be imposed on a business in its first year of operation.
This allows the business time in which to learn the requirements and adapt its activity accordingly.

An effective method for monitoring the changes over time is through the definition of key risk indicators (KRI).
Key risk indicators are quantifiable and measurable variables on which information can be collected and which can be compared over time.
KRIs allow the decision maker to measure the compliance level over a period of time.

Possible KRIs are: number of identified violations, number of complaints received, number compliance programs set, number of indictments filed/fines imposed, number of realized risks (accidents that occurred, infections that were imported from other countries, people that became ill), etc.
Comparing the KRIs to earlier periods provides an indication of whether the supervision system is achieving its objectives.

Once the issues for discourse and the purpose of the consultation have been defined, then the next steps can be taken.
Who should the discourse be held with?

It must also be determined whether it is a good idea to have them meet together or to hold separate meetings for different groups (the public, business proprietors, importers, exporters, employers, employees, experts, etc.).

It is always a good idea to conduct a separate in-house process, that precedes external process, in order to prepare for the public discourse. intra-governmental partners should also participate in the meetings with the public.

How will the discourse be integrated in the process?

Considerations in planning a discourse meeting: Meeting venue and date A meeting venue that is accessible to most of the participants should be arranged.
Consider geographic area, parking, access by public transportation, accessibility for the disabled.
In the appropriate instances, consider going to the participants and being hosted their location.
Also, consider the quality of the meeting venue in terms of atmosphere, acoustics, etc.
These variables can impact the quality of the meetings.
Check the date in advance.
Make sure it does not fall on a religious holiday and that the time is convenient for most of the participants.
Also consider the characteristics of the participants: if they are parents, make sure that schools are open on that day.

If they are members of a specific industry, make sure that the timing fits in with the constraints of the industry (tourism companies are very busy in the summer and over public holidays; the food industry is very busy before major holidays).
Managing the meeting Define in advance who will open the meeting and how it will be conducted (a round of viewpoints, splitting of the time between the questions, who gives the right to speak).
It is important to be aware of and to balance the various interests and the various groups.

It is also vital that weaker groups have the ability to express their position (small businesses, entities that are not incorporated, private individuals, and participants who have difficulty expressing their position).
Define in advance the role that you fulfill: moderator, listening only, and whether you will use another person to help you manage the meeting.
Points of emphasis for the contents of the discourse meeting: Upon the initiation of any discourse, it is important that expectations are coordinated among the participants.
Explain the aim and significance of the discourse.
In what context it is being conducted, and at what stage of the risk management process it is incorporated.
Explain who will use the information given and what influence they have.
It is important to define the topics for discussion, and to define which topics are not open for discussion.
Check the participants' expectations.
Verify that everyone is on the same page regarding the aims of the meeting and its possible impact.
Take into account that some of the participants might want to talk about topics that were not planned for inclusion in the discussion.
Listen with an open mind to suggestions.
Suggestions don't have to be accepted, but it is important to understand these suggestions reflect the motivations of the participants in the discourse.
It is preferable to include them in the discussion to the extent possible.
Summarize briefly at the end of the meeting.
Summarize the main points raised, and in particular, the things that the meeting highlighted that were new.
Mention again what happens from this point on - is this a one-time meeting?
Is a follow-up meeting expected?
Will a summary be circulated?
How will the participants ultimately know that what they said was taken into account?

It is always a good idea to circulate to the participants a summary of the main points raised in the discourse, and express appreciation for their participation in the meeting and the information that they provided.

The quantity of the meetings In situations which separate discussions are held with multiple groups, decide whether to make a concerted effort and hold a series of meetings on the same day or to separate between them.
If the latter, there is time to learn lessons from one meeting to the next.
In cases that appear to require more than one meeting with stakeholders or with a specific group, consider coordinating expectations in advance and preparing accordingly.

Multiple meetings will probably be needed in the following instances: in the case of a highly complex subject or a very broad issue; time is required to thoroughly acquaint the participants with the issues; the discourse is designed to solve a difficult problem; the discourse is designed to formulate a new policy approach or a new way of working.

ANNEX F: COMPARISON OF REGULATORY METHODS AND POLICY TOOLS ACCORDING TO THE DEGREE OF GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION The inverted pyramid presents groups of regulatory methods.
The pyramid is arranged in order of degree of government intervention.
The greater the degree of intervention, the greater the resources required - government and private.
Greater intervention does not guarantee a more effective solution to the risks.
Permits and licenses are the most burdensome regulatory method with the greatest degree of intervention, but additional methods are effective in addressing other risks.
Moreover, there are many risks that this treatment method is not suited for.
It is preferable to start looking for solutions based on the methods at the top of the pyramid.
These incur little government intervention.
The following is a summary description of the various methods specified in figure 14.

Free competition, including due diligence, insurance and professional certification by a third party The terms of free competition provide a broad choice and create an incentive for cautious behavior.
Sometimes a prior government policy has resulted in the creation or amplification of a risk.

Therefore, the option of free competition should be considered, as well as examining whether previous intervention adversely impacts this and prevents the market from operating safely and efficiently.
Systems of free competition can include additional voluntary components: Voluntary disclosure of information.
Problems of information flow and coordination can be resolved by the relevant players taking the initiative and providing information.
Professional qualification by a third party.
The players in a specific field can approach the certification body at their own initiative in order for the body to examine them and grant a certificate of competency.
The certificate does not grant rights but informs the public that the certificate holder complies with standards examined by a third party.
ISO standards are an example.
Insurance and guarantees.
The use of insurance and guarantees enables players to manage their risk by transferring that risk.
As such, if the risk is realized, the injured parties can be compensated.
The advantage of using insurance is that the insurance premium prices insured.
Consequently, the price of the premium encourages the insured to act with greater care.
An example of this can be found in drivers' third- party insurance (insurance that covers property damage caused to a third party).
Advanced regulation nonregulatory tools These methods and tools are designed to change behavior without enforcing compliance by government measures.
Advanced regulations include economic incentives, employing of behavioral economics, and enacting grounds for a civil lawsuit.
Against the backdrop of the discussion on risk, it is important to remember that existing legislation may already address the risk.
To begin with, the general law of torts enables the injured party to sue the party that caused the damage.
Another example is the Israeli Consumer Protection Law and Standard Contracts Law, which provide consumers with a mantle of protection from suppliers who might harm them.

A third example is commercial torts law - designed to prevent commercial losses through the stealing of trade secrets, infringement of intellectual property, passing off, or false use of product names.

Obligatory registration Supervised entities can be required to furnish the government with details about themselves and the supervised activity (name, address, description of the proposed services) before commencement of the activity.
A requirement to register ensures players operating in the field must identify themselves.

This simple requirement can deter problematic players from executing an activity as their details Figure 14: The inverted pyramid - regulatory methods and policy tools according to the degree of government intervention Free competition, including disclosure, insurance and professional certification by a third party Advanced regulation and non- regulatory tools Obligatory registration Government certificate Binding and enforceable rules Binding rules with reporting of commencement of activity Permits and licenses 178 179

Government certificate Using this method, the government issues a certificate stating that a person has specific competencies; however, there is nothing to prevent a person who does not possess the government certificate from engaging in that field.
The use of a specific title is limited only to those who possess the government issued certificate but working in the specific field is also possible without a certificate.
An example of this is accountants: in many countries, any person may engage in accountancy, but only those who received government certification may add the title "certified public" to their name.

Binding and enforceable rules This concerns binding and enforceable rules, the violation of which are punishable; rules such as: prohibition of an activity, duty to act, or conditions regarding the manner of executing the activity.
Binding rules may be in the realm of information: duty of disclosure, obligation to publish, duty to report, or the obligation to record and save information.

Binding rules may impose an obligation on an individual to adopt an internal risk management system - by means of an external standard (for example: ISO 31000 Risk Management), obligation to perform control activities or obligation to have insurance.
Rules require the operation of a governmental supervision and enforcement system.
Binding rules with reporting of commencement of activity A higher level of binding rules includes the duty to report commencement of activity.
This requirement means the government knows who the active players in the field that are subject to the binding rules.
All players must report intent commencement activity prior to implementation of their activity.
This method constitutes a combination of obligatory registration and binding rules.
It is an intermediate level before imposing an obligation to obtain permits and licenses.
Permits and licenses Permits and licenses are the most stringent and comprehensive method of intervention that a government can adopt.
Using them, the government prohibits execution of an act or activity in a field until the party is granted a permit or license.
This method greatly compromises the choices of the individual and requires extensive government and private resources in order to issue individual authorizations.
Therefore, it is recommended the government decision-maker considers this a last resort after all the other methods have been reviewed.
ANNEX G: GUIDELINES FOR CHOOSING REGULATORY METHODS AND POLICY TOOLS The rules presented in this Annex are designed to help adapt the best possible solution to a public problem.
This means the solution is effective in resolving the problem and efficient in terms of the resources that it incurs.
The annex is divided into five sections.
The first section presents various rules of thumb according to the risk characteristics.

Among others, rules are presented for supervision of market entry as opposed to supervision of routine activity; the need to collect information on the supervised entities; handling information-related market failures; handling of concentrated markets and the normative cause of the risk. second section presents regulatory methods and policy tools according to their suitability in different situations.
The tools are divided up according to their competitive impact.
The third section presents rules regarding the information and the public comprehension of the risk.
The better the public understands the risk, the more effective measures it can take to deal with it regardless of regulations or government policy.
The fourth section presents guidelines for using advanced regulation and non-regulatory tools.
This is a set of less well-known methods, and as such, an explanation is provided about when to use them.

In addition, implementations presented improving strengthening the civil lawsuit apparatus, use of behavioral economics, and resolution of problems of coordinated action between multiple parties. fifth section sets out advantages and the disadvantages of the key regulatory methods and policy tools: permits and licenses, binding rules and advanced regulation and non-regulatory tools.

Rules of thumb according to the risk characteristics Treating of risks that emerge during commencement activity versus risks occurring during routine activity: Permits and licenses are suitable when a preliminary check is required before the execution of an activity, while binding rules are imposed on the public throughout the period of execution of the activity (after entry into the market).

The use of permits and licenses is particularly suitable if faced with a high probability risk of great severity, and when the risk results from gaps in competency (knowledge, skills, experience) or from gaps in the equipment (defective or unsuitable equipment).
Permit license-type tools necessitate extensive resources - both from the government and the supervised entities.
Consequently, limiting use them recommended.
In the event of serious risks, both permits and licenses and rules can be used.

Supervision of people and objects as opposed to advance supervision of activities: When those creating the risk are returning players or when a one-time check is required prior to entry into the market - the appropriate tool is licenses for every supervised entity (people or objects).
When those creating the risk are one- time players and an individual check is required before every activity - the appropriate tool is a permit prior to activity.
