Distinction according normative cause of the risk: Force Majeure.
If the risk is due to events beyond human control, society is limited in its ability to affect the risk's realization.
In such cases, the strategy should be to focus on reducing the severity of the losses from the risk and on crisis management.
In some cases, it is also possible to influence the probability of the risk being realized.
It is important to distinguish between rare force majeure events (such as natural disasters) and common events (such as an outbreak of disease).
Market failure.
A major portion of public risk belongs to this category. • The biggest group of market failures includes externalities (or "external influences").
An externality occurs when a person performs an action and the price of the action falls on others.
Pollution is a classic example of an externality as the risk is dispersed and is not internalized by the polluter.
In the case of externalities, the executor of the activity does not bear all the risk and the costs incurred.
Consequently, they might execute the activity excessively without taking the appropriate precautions.
The purpose of the regulations or the public policy is to cause the creator of the risk to internalize the implications of their action.

When this is not feasible, the aim will be to prevent them from creating excessive risk (and effectively cause the creator of the risk to act as if they had internalized the implications of their actions).
The main tool to this end is not regulatory - civil lawsuits enable individuals to claim compensation from whoever caused them damage.
As such, one should examine the civil lawsuit mechanism and whether it could mitigate the risk.

When the externalities cause heavy damage, adding a regulatory layer can be considered, as well as establishing provisions obliging the creator of the damage to take various precautions. • In the event of a market failure resulting from a problem in the flow of information (partial or asymmetric information), solution should focus on improving the flow of information.
Sometimes advanced regulations nonregulatory tools can be used.
For example: in the event of an information gap between a supplier and a consumer a presumption can be enacted.

The presumption is a legal rule according to which a certain fact can be assumed, without the need to prove it, in favor of the party at a disadvantage due to the fact they possess inferior information.

Such a rule may enable the weak party (in terms of the information in its possession) to sue the strong party even in individual check before each activity, this rule may place a heavy burden both on the supervising agency issuing the permits and on the supervised entities.

To illustrate the difference between the license burden and the permit burden, contrast the number of drivers in Israel with the amount of times a year a driver crosses a junction; or the number of importers in Israel as opposed to the number of imported shipments to Israel each year.
Permits are particularly suitable in the case of a market that has few activities, where each one creates a high risk.

In view of the heavy burden involved in conducting an individual check before every activity, it is advisable to examine converting the regime of permits and licenses into a combination of binding rules and the duty to report before executing the activity creating the risk.
In this way, the decision-maker defines a binding requirement and even receives information in advance about the dangerous activities.
This way, the decision-maker can choose on which ones to conduct supervision activities.
Need supervised entities order address the risk: If there is a need for information about the supervised entities in order to monitor the risk, duty to report is the most appropriate tool.
When enforcement system needs information on the identity of the supervised entities or on their characteristics, there is no need to establish a regime of licenses, permits, etc..

It is often possible to convert a regime of permits and licenses into binding rules (design standards or performance standards) in combination with a duty to report commencement of activity or entry into the market.
When information is required both by the supervised entity and the public, the duty to report can be expanded and obligatory registration can be defined.

Obligatory registration includes collection of information on the supervised entities in a database ("register") that is publicly accessible, and the conditions defined in respect thereof (for example: Registrar Companies, Pawns Registrar, Contractors Registrar, and Databases Registrar).
Handling with information-related market failings: To resolve a problem of gaps in between parties, use should be made of duty to disclose or obligation to publish.

Another option that can make information publicly accessible is to impose a duty to report and an obligation to publish information to the public (for example: to publish data about the financial strength of insurance companies or to publish the safety rankings of the supervised entities.

When the public lacks information about the risks or ways of dealing with them, use can be made of campaigns, training, providing information and communication of the risks or the means of dealing with them.

Handling of concentrated markets: In dealing with concentrated markets, it is preferable not to use tools such as permits and licenses because they create entry barriers and exacerbate the structural problem.
In the case of concentrated markets, use of binding rules or advanced regulations is preferable.

For example, if the public mistakenly thinks that the damage from a given risk can be mitigated by using tools or specific equipment, it will invest resources in solutions that are not applicable.
It is important to make the risk characteristics (its causes, when and where it is realized, and which players are involved in creating the risk), clear to the public.
Here too, it is a matter of information and understanding the risk, as such, the first thing to do is to consider tools that improve the transfer of information to the public.
In this context, it is a good idea to examine just how complex the issue is, and the capacity of the relevant audience to understand it.
When large businesses and knowledge-intensive companies suffer from knowledge gaps, it is easy to provide them with the information and the implications in respect of the risk.

Conversely, when the information about the risk is abstract, complex, or requires professional knowledge to understand it, (especially when the information is intended for the public and not for professionals), providing information may not be an effective alternative.
In such cases other tools should be examined, for example, mandating the use of protective measures against the risk.
As stated in the section on "Risk Communication", the choice of mandatory regulation and the reasons behind it must also be explained to the public.
Guidelines using advanced regulation and non-regulatory tools Advanced regulations are particularly well-suited to treating risk that is not severe.
When the risk is not typically severe or highly probable, and there are no serious compliance problems advance regulations maybe more effective than traditional regulations.
Since most of the public are law- abiding and the major portion of risks are not severe, advanced regulation is a solution for a wide range of situations.
It provides simple solutions without the need to establish a supervision and enforcement system, where the origin of the risks is in a normative population.
Consequently, advanced regulation provides an economical solution in terms of resources.
It enable the decision-maker to concentrate on imposing restrictions focused on the severe risks and on instances of wrongdoing.
Advanced regulation may solution when deciding between a risk acceptance strategy and a risk mitigation strategy.
In those instances, use can be made of advanced regulation, and even combined with preparations for crisis management.

Advanced regulation may be added as another layer, as a tool that encourages compliance by providing positive reinforcement (for example: traffic police who hand out positive tickets for careful and safe driving).
When the aim of the policy is to grant a specific group financial aid or an 186 187
economic incentive, it is preferable to do so directly and as simply as possible.
A complicated policy with indirect payments and benefits may miss their goal and create undesirable results.

For example: a study by the Bank of Israel and the Central Bureau of Statistics examined the impact of rental assistance grants provided by the Jerusalem Municipality to students who live in the city center.
According to the study, the grants led to a rise in rents in the city center.
The implication: part of the student assistance was passed homeowners.
Furthermore, the grants led to a rise in rent for those renting apartments who had not received a grant.

Improving strengthening mechanism of civil lawsuits: Civil lawsuits are the most widely used tool for restraining risky behavior: they enable compensation for the injured party and serve to deter the creator of the risk. • In the case of minor damage that does not require full, costly, and lengthy legal proceedings, a claim can be filed with the Small Claims Court.

This is a simple, expedited procedure, so even someone not represented by a lawyer can sue for damage. • In order to enable a civil lawsuit apparatus, a defined right must be enacted so that the injured party can sue in respect of it.

The legal remedy may be financial compensation, or a restrictive order prohibiting the creator of the risk from acting. • If there is difficulty in proving substantial financial damage, exemplary damages can awarded.
This mechanism enables the victim to receive compensation without proving damage.

It also defines the maximum compensation that can be awarded without proof of damage. • Sometimes, the concern is that because the damage is spread, the injured parties will not have the incentive to sue.
This occurs when damage is dispersed across a wide population and each of the injured parties only absorbs a small portion of the damage.
The solution in these cases may be to grant the option of instituting a class action on behalf of the injured group.
This mechanism enables one of the injured parties to serve as a representative plaintiff and institute the class action on behalf of all injured parties.
The rule in Israeli law is you have to opt out i.e. by default, all members of the group are represented, but they can take active steps not to be included in it.

This mechanism enables a wide group of injured parties who have sustained dispersed damage to institute a unified action (generally a large one) that justifies legal proceedings creates a considerable deterrent for the creator of the damage. • In event evidentiary difficulties in proving the damage or the causal connection between the unacceptable behavior and damage, evidentiary rules can be enacted.
One of the most commonly used rules includes presumptions provisions about transferring burden of proof.
As a rule, the plaintiff must persuade the court that its argument is more reasonable than that of the defendant.
Presumption is an evidentiary tool stipulating the burden of persuasion lies with the defendant.
Presumptions can bridge inequalities in access to evidence and can simplify the legal proceedings.

For example: Section 39 of the Israel Torts Ordinance stipulates that in a fire damage claim, the defendant (as the owner of the real estate from which the fire emanated), must prove that the fire was not caused by negligence on their part (and is not the responsibility of the plaintiff).
Similarly, Israeli Standard Contracts Law stipulates a list of conditions that are presumed to be depriving and therefore invalid.
By virtue of the presumption, the plaintiff is not required to prove that those conditions are depriving.
Transfer of the burden of proof by presumption can resolve problems evidentiary difficulties enable injured parties to file a civil lawsuit against the risk creators.

Guiding behavior by means behavioral economics: • Economic theory analyzes human behavior on the basis of the assumption that human beings make rational decisions (i.e. define their goals and make decisions that advance these goals in the best possible manner).
Behavioral economics branch investigates systematic deviation from the making of "rational" decisions.
Such deviations are also called bias. • Behavioral economics offers a tool set that enables government to influence the behavior of individuals.
Behavioral economics can be used to support the decision-making process of the individual, without obligating the individual to do or avoid doing something. • One behavioral method is boosting.
This method focuses on irrational decision-making as a result of incomplete information and an inability to process and analyze it.
This method encourages giving the public the tools to improve their decision-making process.
An example is imparting knowledge and an understanding of financial concepts in order to improve the financial decisions made by the public. • Another method is called nudge.
Nudge is designed to shape the decision-making environment of individuals in order to influence their decision simply inexpensively, without limiting their freedom of choice.
Not only can can use nudge to influence the decision- making process of the individual, so can commercial entities.
In the commercial sector, an example of this is making consumers agree to accept advertisements as their default setting.
It is therefore sometimes necessary to "amend" existing use of nudge that produces an undesirable result.

Examples of nudge are: simplifying complex decisions (especially in the case of uncommon decisions that the individual has little experience of); mapping comparing alternatives (a concrete and clear- cut description of the alternatives and their implications, clear-cut presentation of comparable criteria) and defining a default (people tend not to deviate from the status quo, hence the default has great potency).
A third method eliminating behavioral bias (debiasing).
This method focuses on the root causes of problems of bounded rationality, such as partial information and cognitive limitations in processing and analyzing information.

Behavioral debiasing is achieved by identifying the factors contributing to the bias and then modifying those factors in order to weaken them (solving problems of a lack of information, or an environment that contributes to distorted decision- making) or providing about those factors in order to help the public avoid those biases. 188 189
Resolving problems of coordinated action: • Sometimes risks stem from an inability to act in coordination or in sync.

In such instances, the public has several options, but no unequivocal preference for a specific one; however, it is important the public act in a concerted manner according to the same rule or method. • The preferred way of dealing with problems of coordination is to employ informal (nonbinding) standards.
These standards do not impose a binding standard on the market, but they help all players converge on a uniform method.
Together players, the government provides the market with the foundations for coordination and may also encourage voluntary adoption of a higher standard.
One example is the layout of the keys on a computer keyboard: both manufacturers and consumers have an interest in the existence of a defined recognized standard everyone can work according to.
The generally accepted layout is QWERTY.

In the United States an alternative layout called Dvorak is also recognized. • When problems of coordination create significant risks (in terms of severity and probability), use can also be made of binding rules.
An example is the rule to drive on the right side of the road.
Driving on the right does not have any real advantage over driving on the left, but to ensure public safety, a binding and uniform rule must be established that everyone abides by.

Advantages disadvantages according to groups of regulatory methods and policy tools Permits and licenses: Advantages In this regime, execution of the supervised activity prohibited without advance receipt an individual license or permit from the regulator.
The main advantage of this group is the tight control afforded the government over the supervised activity.

Furthermore, the obligation to operate under a government permit or license enables the State to revoke the permit or license (in the event of a breach), and thereby terminate the activity of the offending party.
Disadvantages The typical disadvantage of the permits and licenses group lies in government intervention in the supervised activity.
The government has to authorize every supervised entity or supervised activity (as the case may be).
These tools create considerable friction between the government and the public, as every activity requires an individual permit or license.
Operation of these tools generally requires a bureaucratic apparatus - submission of documents, checks before and after, and issuing of the permits and licenses.

All these impose a regulatory burden on the public (expressed in direct costs, indirect costs and market entry barriers), and necessitate allocation of substantial government resources in order to manage the bureaucratic apparatus that supports this method.
In addition, as with all government intervention, permits and licenses impose compliance costs on the public.
Binding rules: Advantages The advantages of binding rules are that they can be defined to regulate or monitor activity without the need for active State intervention.
In this regime, the State establishes rules and enforces them, but the public does not have to engage with the State or obtain a permit or license.
Binding rules are enforceable, and the government resources required are exclusively enforcement purposes.
Disadvantages As in the permits and licenses group, binding rules constitute traditional regulation including obligations restrictions.
Compliance obligations carries an economic price (purchase of equipment, execution of processes).
The restrictions and prohibitions may partially block or prevent beneficial activities.
Binding rules are based on supervision and enforcement during the execution of the activity; consequently, government is unable to inspect compliance with the requirements in advance.

Advanced regulation non- regulatory tools: Advantages The advantages of this group are the flexibility and suitability of the tools, the implementation of which is not enshrined in legal provisions mandated by the State.
Individuals are free to choose, and implementation is custom tailored on a case-by-case basis.
Tools in this group impose very few restrictions on the freedom of the individual and on socioeconomic activities.
In addition, related tools can be used to resolve a wide variety of failures by educating and empowering the relevant parties.
Disadvantages Use of the tools in this group diminishes government control compared to traditional regulation.
In addition, guiding behavior with soft power, such as incentive systems may have indirect, hidden, and unpredictable results.
Furthermore, some of these tools necessitate government resources - from providing grants and tax benefits, to educational campaigns and making the information publicly accessible. 190 191
Regulation, and government policy in particular, may remove barriers to competition or strengthen them.
Preventing harm to competition is essential in order to reduce prices, bring about higher quality, more variety in products and services, and contribute to productivity.
To examine the impact of regulation or public policy on competition, it is first necessary to identify which markets the decision will impact.

In order to do so, the following questions need to be asked: • Which businesses are involved? • Who are their customers? • What are the relevant products/ services? • What are the characteristics of the players? (large/ small, imports/ domestic/ exports/ existing/ new that may enter the market) • Will regulation impact additional/ related markets?
An illustrative example: regulation of the supplier market may impact the distributor market.
Regulation stipulating that a supplier can only operate within a 50 km radius of its logistics center limits every supplier to a defined geographic area.
As a result of the geographic restriction on suppliers, results in the distributors (who buy from suppliers and sell to consumers) in each area are reliant on a single supplier.
The distributors are hurt by the market strength of a single supplier as well as by the absence of product variety.

Following are issues that increase concerns about harm competition: • In a concentrated market with few competitors, careful consideration must be given to the possible of harming competition (a simple rule of thumb is that a concentrated market is usually one with up to five players). • The following types of policy arise increased concerns about harming competition: price control, production quotas (limiting and allotting quantities), import quotas defining industry layout (size of competitors, number of competitors).

Small and medium- size businesses bear the burden of regulation more as they are smaller and more vulnerable. "Small businesses": employ up to 20 workers and have an annual turnover of up to ILS 10 million. "Medium-size businesses": employ up to 100 workers and have an annual turnover of up to ILS 100 million.
Small and medium-size businesses (SMBs) make a decisive contribution to the economy.
In Israel, SMBs constitute 99.2% of all businesses, provide work for 70% of the employed, and contribute about half the economy's added value.

Regulation and public policy may impact SMBs directly and indirectly (for example: when the regulation provides large business, but also has an impact on the suppliers or on its business customers who are SMBs).

The guiding principle is to think first of the small businesses (Think Small First) - to formulate rules based on how small businesses will be impacted by them and examine costs from their perspective.
Examining risks that SMBs create Strive to take the constraints and vulnerabilities of SMBs into account, subject to the risk assessment and to the influence of SMBs on the creation of the risks.

To this end, clarify and examine: • Does activity SMBs contribute to the creation of the risks that need to be addressed? • What is the scale of the risk (frequency, severity economic damage) that might be created by SMBs?
